transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood, I think Tomas is on as well, he'll walk through the code examples and infra bits. quick note: we'll be recording.
[00:18] Tomás Rivera (SE): hi all, Tomás here. we'll do a short demo in both Python and TypeScript, show auth, env setup, and then the console optimize hints. feel free to interrupt.
[00:34] Sophie Wu (Apex): hi. we have Helen, Amir and me. main goal is to understand how fast we can get an integration working and what the security concerns are.
[00:44] Helen Park (CTO): yes, timeline is end of Q1 if feasible. we need CI-friendly secrets, and likely on-prem options for PII workloads.
[00:53] Amir Qureshi (Infra): also want to understand latency/cost tradeoffs, and whether we can use our KMS for keys.
[01:05] Jordan: great. quick agenda: 1) quick auth and SDK quickstart, 2) env patterns for local and CI + Docker, 3) console/Optimize walkthrough, 4) Q&A and next steps.
[01:20] Tomás: i'll start with the python snippet. so, a minimal flow: pip install redwood-client, set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your env, and then from redwood import Client, client = Client(api_key=os.environ["REDWOOD_API_KEY"]). then client.chat.create(prompt=...). super small.
[01:42] Sophie: is API key the recommended path? we use SSO, and don't want long-lived keys in dev machines.
[01:50] Jordan: good question. recommended for dev/proof-of-concept is short-lived service tokens or personal tokens with scoped permissions. for prod we suggest using service accounts plus your KMS + short lived tokens (we support OIDC flows and SAML SSO mapping to roles).
[02:08] Amir: typo in our notes, do you support AWS KMS or GCP KMS?
[02:13] Tomás: yes both; Redwood can integrate with customer KMS via our private deployments or via dedicated using KMS integrations. there is a slight caveat: for hosted we manage key material but we also support customer-managed keys for Enterprise.
[02:28] Speaker 1 (auto): little bit of echo there.
[02:33] Helen: on private deploys, can you run completely air-gapped?
[02:37] Jordan: yes, our private package supports on-prem air-gapped installs. there are some additional ops reqs like image repositories and license keys. we'll send the onboarding checklist.
[02:49] Tomás: jumping back to code. in TypeScript it's similar: import {RedwoodClient} from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); then await client.generate(...). we also show an example using fetch with the REST API for serverless functions.
[03:10] Sophie: do you have a sample for GitHub Actions so we don't expose keys?
[03:15] Tomás: yes, recommended pattern: store REDWOOD_API_KEY as repo secret, in Actions you reference secrets.REDWOOD_API_KEY and set env in the job. for ephemeral credentials we have a token-exchange endpoint pattern; we'll include a sample.
[03:31] Amir: what about Docker images? we want to build images that embed minimal runtime and don't bake creds.
[03:36] Tomás: put keys in runtime env, use entrypoint to pull from a secret store (e.g. AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault). in Dockerfiles we avoid ENV with keys; use ARG for build-time only. in the sample repo we show a multi-stage build.
[03:52] Jordan: quick detour to Console — i'll share my screen.
[03:58] Speaker 2 (bad attrib): (screen share noise)
[04:03] Jordan: so here's the Console model page, you can pin model variants, set rollout policies, set autoscale for dedicated pools. we also show token-level cost breakdowns and latency histograms per route.
[04:20] Helen: can we restrict who can change rollouts?
[04:24] Jordan: yes RBAC — roles for developers, SREs, and admins. SSO/SAML integrated for enterprise; audit logs capture overrides.
[04:33] Sophie: what's the level of observability for token breakdowns? we need per-request payloads for debugging.
[04:40] Jordan: Console shows token counts and breakdowns. for deeper tracing we have tracing hooks that you can ingest into your existing APM. logs and traces can be exported to customer-owned storage for retention and compliance.
[04:55] Tomás: back to Optimize — we recommend three levers: batching, prefix/KV caching, and quantization/variant selection. for example, when you have short chat turns you can enable continuous batching with a small latency budget; that drops per-token cost significantly.
[05:12] Amir: do you auto-tune batching?
[05:14] Tomás: Optimize gives suggestions based on your observed distribution and you can apply them or run experiments. suggestions include recommended batch sizes, a suggested quantization level (e.g., 8-bit for dev traffic), and cache TTLs for prefix caching.
[05:30] Sophie: can we see an example where cost went down and latency stayed within SLOs?
[05:35] Tomás: yes i'll share a before/after. (screenshare) this customer had median latency 180ms, after batching + prefix caching they were at 130ms and 30% lower token cost. it's workload dependent but it's typical.
[05:50] Speaker 3 (auto): small transcription error, says 1 80 ms but meant 180.
[05:57] Helen: curious about model routing — can you route by region to keep data in EU?
[06:02] Jordan: yes policy-based routing by geo, tier, or even customer label. you can pin a tenant to EU-hosted nodes. that ties into data residency.
[06:12] Amir: security — do we get full request-level logs, or are they redacted?
[06:18] Jordan: you can enable full raw logs in Private/Dedicated deployments per the retention policy; for Hosted we provide tokenized logs and allow exporting to customer buckets for long-term retention. personally identifiable info should be redacted at ingestion — we provide filters and pre-ingest hooks.
[06:36] Sophie: quick question on tokenization — do you provide embeddings and search support?
[06:40] Tomás: yes generative APIs plus embeddings endpoint; we also have optimized reranking. we'll point to the embedding usage guide.
[06:50] Jordan: jumping back to the repo — Tomás do you want to walk through the project tree?
[06:55] Tomás: sure. repo has /py-example and /ts-example. both include Dockerfile, GH Actions workflow, and a sample serverless function. important files: .env.example, README with REDWOOD_API_KEY usage, and a security.md with recommended KMS patterns.
[07:13] Sophie: i saw a mention of prefix caching — is that client-side or server-side?
[07:18] Tomás: server-side. Redwood's runtime manages KV caches for prefix tokens (like histories) so repeated prompts can be cached and served faster. client can opt-in to using the cache or bypass it for sensitive requests.
[07:30] Amir: are model weights or cache stored in customer's infrastructure on private deploys?
[07:36] Jordan: in private/on-prem options you control storage; caches can be local to the customer's cluster. for Dedicated we can configure placement to ensure data isolation.
[07:47] Helen: what's the usual pilot size? i.e., how many requests per second?
[07:51] Jordan: pilots range from low traffic tens RPS to medium hundreds; we size Dedicated pools based on concurrency requirements. our trial credit can cover some pilot runs.
[08:03] Sophie: do you handle rate limiting per token or per request?
[08:07] Tomás: both. Console allows per-api-key rate limits, per-route quotas and organization-level budgets.
[08:15] Amir: curious about fallback policies — say a primary region has outage, does it fail open to another model variant?
[08:22] Jordan: yes you can configure fallback to a cheaper model or alternative region with graceful degradation. automatic fallback respects SLO policies.
[08:32] Sophie: (soft laugh) okay we like fallback, but we want to test it.
[08:36] Tomás: we can script failure injection during the benchmark.
[08:40] Jordan: now, let's do a quick live example in Python hitting the hosted endpoint from a lambda-like environment. i'll paste the code in chat.
[08:46] Speaker 4 (auto): code paste coming through.
[08:50] Tomás: note the sample uses a short-lived token exchange: you call your auth service, it mints a short token scoped to the route. avoids long-lived keys in lambdas.
[09:02] Sophie: can you show the CI workflow snippet?
[09:05] Tomás: sure. (reads) name: ci; on: push; jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest; env: REDWOOD_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.REDWOOD_API_KEY }}. steps: checkout, setup python/node, run tests. that's it.
[09:23] Amir: if we rotate keys frequently will that break running pods?
[09:27] Tomás: you should design token lifetimes to be short and use sidecar or secret-sync to rotate without restarts. we have examples for Kubernetes using CSI drivers.
[09:38] Helen: on compliance: does Redwood provide SOC2 and penetration test results?
[09:42] Jordan: yes we'll send the SOC2 report and pen test summary. for Enterprises we also do security workshops and can accommodate certain audit requests.
[09:53] Sophie: would Dedicated be needed for our PII workflows?
[09:56] Jordan: possibly — Dedicated gives data isolation and customer-owned infrastructure options; Private is fully air-gapped. we can scope based on data classification.
[10:06] Tomás: for cost tuning, we usually recommend starting hosted to iterate and then move to Dedicated once you have throughput and SLOs nailed down.
[10:15] Amir: any limitations on model quantization or plugin libs?
[10:19] Tomás: some model variants perform better under certain quantization; we have validated matrix per model/quant level. plugin libraries like custom tokenizers can be shipped in Private deployments.
[10:30] Sophie: let's try the hands-on now — Jordan, can you make a new sandbox org for us?
[10:34] Jordan: yes i can provision a sandbox with free credits. i'll need primary contact.
[10:38] Helen: that's me. helen@apexanalytics.com.
[10:42] Jordan: noted. i'll provision and send access by tomorrow.
[10:47] Tomás: ok i'll drop the repo link in chat — it has step-by-step: set REDWOOD_API_KEY, run python -m examples.chat, or npm run dev for TS. also includes sample benchmark script using wrk.
[10:59] Sophie: will the repo include sample configs for Optimize tuning?
[11:02] Tomás: yes a config.yaml example with batching and cache TTL presets per workload.
[11:08] Amir: i'd like to run a latency benchmark from our EU infra — can you support that?
[11:12] Jordan: yes we'll schedule a 30 minute session and coordinate test endpoints; we'll also show how to configure regional routing.
[11:20] Sophie: any notes about logging PII? we want to ensure logs don't contain raw user messages in hosted mode.
[11:26] Jordan: hosted mode redacts per policy; we can set higher redaction and route raw logs to your bucket if you need them, but that's recommended only for private/dedicated when you control retention.
[11:39] Helen: what's the SLA for Dedicated?
[11:42] Jordan: Dedicated has SLA options up to 99.9% and we offer premium support tiers.
[11:49] Speaker 5 (auto): minor mis-transcribe: 'nine nine nine' vs 'nine nine point nine' noted.
[11:55] Tomás: quick demo wrap: the repo shows env patterns: .env.example, ci/workflows, Docker multi-stage, sample trust boundary doc.
[12:05] Jordan: ok let's capture next steps. Sophie, you want SOC2 and repo, Tomas will publish repo. schedule benchmark week of 2/10. any additional asks?
[12:18] Sophie: include a sample SAML config for Okta if possible.
[12:22] Amir: include a note about secret rotation patterns for k8s.
[12:26] Jordan: will do.
[12:30] Helen: timeline — we'll try pilot in early March if benchmarks look good.
[12:36] Jordan: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the pack and links.
[12:42] Speaker 6 (auto): meeting ended.
